(1851 - 1935)
Andrew Cecil Bradley was an English literary scholar best remembered for his work on Shakespeare.
He was born in Surrey, England. Harold Bloom has paid tribute to Bradley's place in the great tradition of critical writing on Shakespeare.
Bradley's two major works are - Shakespearean Tragedy (1904) and Oxford Lectures on Poetry (1909).
All his published works was originally delivered in the form of lectures. His Gifford lectures at the university of Glasgow (1907 - 08) was entitled "Ideals of Religion".
"Shakespearean Tragedy" is a series of lectures by Bradley on Hamlet, Othello, King Lear & Macbeth.

(1929 - 1945)
Anne Frank was a German diarist and writer.
She was a holocaust convict of the Nazi movement in Germany.
Her war time diary "The Diary of a Young Girl" has been the basis for several plays and films.
In 1941 she lost her citizenship and became stateless.
She died in 1945 in World War II.
"The Diary of a Young Girl" chronicles her life from 12th June 1942 to 1st Aug 1944.
The diary was first published in Germany and France in 1950.
Quote by Anne Frank: "When I write I can shake off all my cares. My sorrow disappears, my spirits are revived. But, and that's a big question, will I ever be able to write something great, will I ever become a journalist or a writer?"

Bapsi Sidhwa is a Pakistani novelist who writes in English but is a resident in America. She won Highest Pakistan's National Honour "SITARA - I - IMTIAZ".
She is best known for her collaborative work with Indo Canadian film-maker Deepa Mehta. Sidhwa wrote both "Ice Candy Man" (1991 novel) and "Water: A Novel (2006 novel) for Deepa Mehta's film.
She was born in Karachi and is presently living in United States.
The other important novels are "The Pakistani Bride", "The Crow Eaters", "An American Brat" and "Cracking India" (US - 1991, India - 1992, England - 1988).

(1857-1913)
Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist and semiotician whose idea laid a foundation for many significant developments both in linguistic and semiology in 20th century.
He is widely considered as one of the fathers of 20th century linguistics and one of two major fathers (together with Charles Sanders Peirce) of Semiotics/Semiology.
In Europe the most important work in this period of influence was done by the Prague School. Saussure formulated four major dichotomies in his Course in General Linguistics i.e. Langue-Parole, Synchrony dictionary, Paradigmatic-Syntagmatic and Signifier -Signified.
In America Saussure's idea informed the distributionalism of Leonard Bloomfield.
Saussure's most influential work Course General Linguistics was published posthumously in 1916 by former students Charles Bally and Albert Sechehafe on the basis of notes taken from Saussure's lecture in Geneva from 1906-1912.
It is seminal linguistic work.
He is the pioneer of Structuralism.
Saussure's sign and Bakhtin's dialogism helped Julia Kristeva to derive "Intertextuality".
He stated that "The birth and death of a Language are not subject to human language" in his work Words upon Words as "The actual birth of a new language has never reported in the World" because "We have never known of a Language which was not spoken the day before or which was not spoken in the same way day before".

(1759-1805)
Johann Christoph Friedrich Von Schiller was a Germen poet, philosopher, historian and playwright.
During the last seventeen years of his life (1788-1805), Schiller produced his productive works.
The relationship between Schiller and Goethe and their discussion on aesthetics led to a period referred to as Weimar Classicism.
Goethe and Schiller worked together on "Xenien", a collection of short satirical poems in which both of them challenged opponents to their philosophical visions.
He was named after king "Fredrick the Great" but he was called Fritz by nearly everyone.
At school he wrote his first play "The Robbers", which dramatizes the conflict between the two aristocratic brothers : the elder, Moor leads a group of rebellious students into the Bohemian forest where they become Robin Hood- like bandit while the younger, Franz Moor schemes to inherit his father's considerable estate.
This play was inspired by Leisewitz's earlier play "Julius of Tarent" a favourite of Schiller.
In 1789, he was appointed professor of History and Philosophy in Jena, where he wrote only historical works.
Schiller and Goethe founded 'Weimer Theater' which became the leading theater in Germany.
For his achievements, Schiller was ennobled in 1802 by the Duke of Weimar, adding the nobiliary particle "von" to his name.
The first significant biography of Schiller was by his sister-in-law Caroline von Wolzogen in 1830.
Schiller said "art is the daughter of freedom".

(1877-1962)
Hermann Karl Hesse was a German born Swiss poet, novelist and painter.
His best known works include :.
Steppenwolf.
Siddhartha and.
The Glass Bead Game.
Each of these novels explores an individual's search for authenticity, self-knowledge and spirituality.
In 1946 he received Nobel prize in literature.
In his Juvenilia collection "Gerbersau", Hesse describes experiences and anecdotes from his childhood and youth in Claw (Hesse's favorites place). He felt signs of serious depression at the first year at school.
In 1896, his poem "Madonna "appeared in a Viennese periodical and he released his small volume of poetry "Romantic Songs".
In 1898 his "One Hour After Midnight" was published, that was written to please his wife.
His first breakthrough as a writer was his first novel "Peter Camenzind" which appeared in 1904.
His second novel "Beneath the Wheel" was published in 1906, and "Gertrude" in 1910.
His masterpiece "Siddhartha" (1922) was derived from Hesse's interest in Schopenhauer (philosophy and Theosophy). This masterpiece was a product of Hesse's interest in India.
In 1914,during the First World War, when he registered himself with the Imperial Army, he wrote an essay "O Friends, Not These Tone", through which he appealed to his fellow intellectuals not to fall for a nationalistic madness and hatred.
His novella, Siddhartha showed the love for Indian culture and Buddhist philosophy that had already developed earlier in his life.
In 1923, he received Swiss citizenship.
His next major works 'Kurgast' (1925) and 'The Nuremberg Trip' (1927) were the autobiographical narratives. His novel 'Steppenwolf' was published in 1927.
On his 50th birthday , Hugo ball a friend of Hesse wrote his first biography.
His last work "Glass Bead Game " was published in 1943 in Switzerland.
He used the pen name Emil Sinclair while writing Demian (1919).

(1901 - 1981)
Jacques Morie Emile Lacan was a French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist who has been called "The most controversial psycho-analyst since Freud".
He's ideas had a significant impact on Critical Theory, Literary Theory, Linguistic Theory, 20th century French Philosophy, Sociology, Feminist theory, Film theory and Clinical Psychoanalysis.
He was especially interested in the philosophies of Karl Napiers and Martin Heidegger.
He stated that - "I think therefore I am as, I am not where I think and I think where I am not."
In the four fundamental concepts of Psychoanalysis Lacan argues that "every unsuccessful act is a successful not to say well-turned, discourse."
For Lacan - "Unconscious' structured like a language".

1. Return to Freud: Lacan's Return to Freud emphasises a renewed attention to the original text of Freud and included a radical critique of Ego Psychology. Whereas, Lacan's quarrel with the object relations psychoanalysis was a more muted affair. 2. Me Mirror Stage: It is a concept in the psychoanalytic theory of Jacques Lacan. It is based on the belief that infants recognise themselves in a mirror (literal) or other symbolic contraption which induces apperception from the age of 6 months.
Foucault described it as Formative of the function of the / as revealed in psychoanalytic experience. 3. Three Orders (a) The Real:.
It refers to that which is authentic, unchangeable truth in reference both to being the self and the external dimension of experience. (b) The Symbolic:.
With the increasing prominence of the Symbolic in Lacan's thought after 1953, the Imaginary becomes viewed in a rather different light, as structured by the symbolic order. It is still the case that "the body in pieces finds its unity in the image of the other ... [or] its own specular image" but no longer does "analysis consist in the imaginary realisation of the subject ... to make it well-rounded, this ego, to ... have definitely integrated all its disjointed fragmentary states, its scattered limbs, its pregenital phases, its partial drives". Instead, "one finds a guide beyond the imaginary, on the level of the symbolic plane" (c) Imaginary:.
The basis of the Imaginary order is the formation of the ego in the "mirror stage"; by articulating the ego in this way "the category of the imaginary provides the theoretical basis for a long-standing polemic against ego-psychology" on Lacan's part. Since the ego is formed by identifying with the counterpart or specular image, "identification" is an important aspect of the imaginary. The relationship whereby the ego is constituted by identification is a locus of "alienation", which is another feature of the imaginary, and is fundamentally narcissistic: thus Lacan wrote of "the different phases of imaginary, narcissistic, specular identification - the three adjectives are equivalent" which make up the ego's history.

John Crow Ransom was an American educator scholar and literary critic, poet, essayist and editor.
He is considered to be the founder of 'New Criticism' (through his work "New Criticism" in 1941). In the work he insisted that criticism should be based on a study of "Structure & Texture".
He was the first editor and founder of the Kenyon Review (1939).
His first volumes of Poem "Poems about God" (1919) was praised by Robert Frost and Robert Graves.
In 1930, alongside 11 other Southern Agrarians, he published the conservative, Agrarian Manifest - I'll Take My Stand: The South and the Agrarian Tradition.
Ransom's literary reputation is based chiefly on two collections of poetry:.
Chills and Fever (1924) and.
Two Gentlemen in Bonds (1927)
Ransom's book "The New Criticism" organized the principles of New Criticism in which he emphasized close reading of a text and talks about 'total structure and local texture'.
In 1951, Ransom won Bollingen Prize for Poetry and his 1963 "Selected Poems" received national book award in 1964.
Ransom is an influential critic associated with three important theories and critical movements 1. The Fugitives (One who is escaping persecution) 2. Agrarianism (a Philosophy that advocates the equal distribution of land) 3. New Criticism Collection of Poems 1. Chills and Fever (1924)

(1941 -)
Julia Kristeva is a Bulgarian - French Philosopher, literary critic, psychoanalyst, feminist and most recently a novelist.
She is now a professor at the University of Paris Diderot.
Kristeva became influential in International critical analysis, cultural theory and feminism after publishing her first book Semeiotike (1969).
She is also the founder and head of the Simone de Beauvoir Prize committee.
On 2nd August 1967, Kristeva married the novelist Phillipe Sallers.
She travelled to China in 1970's and later wrote "About Chinese Women" (1977)
Her "Semiotic" is closely related to the infantile pre-oedipal referred to in the work of Freud, Otto Rank, Melanie Klein, British Object Relation psychoanalysis, and Lacan's pre-mirror stage.
Kristeva is also known for her adoption of Plato's idea of the 'Chora' (meaning - a nourishing maternal space ) (2011).
She is also noted for her work on the concept of 'Intertextuality' (It is the shaping of a text's meaning by another text). It is derived from Bakhtin's Dialogism and Saussure's Sign.
Kristeva is regarded as a key proponent of French Feminism together with Simone de Beauvoir, Hélène Cixous, and Luce Irigaray.
Kristeva made a famous disambiguation of three types of feminism in "Women's Time" in New Maladies of the Soul (1993).
She proposed the idea of 'Multiple Sexual Identities' against the joint code of "Unified Feminine Language" .
She was awarded the Holberg International Memorial Prize (2004) and Hannah Arendt prize (2006) for Political Thought.
In Intellectual Impostures (1997) by Alan Sokal and Jean Bricmont, devote a chapter to Julia's use of Mathematics in her writing.
Julia Kristeva coined the term "Intertextuality" in 1966 explaining that there are two relationships going on whenever we read a text; (i) There is a relationship between us and author (x-axis) & (ii) Between the text and other texts (y-axis or vertical axis) The vertical axis gives us the definition of Intertextuality.

Kenneth Burke was an American theorist who had powerful impact on 20th century Philosophy, Aesthetics, criticism and theatrical theory.
Burke is best known for his analyses based on the nature of knowledge.
He was the first individual to view literature as symbolic action,.
In "Definition of Man", the first essay of his collection Language as Symbolic Action (1966), Burke defined humankind as "Symbol using animal".
This definition of man means - "Reality has actually been built up for us through noting but our symbol system".
He was influenced by the idea of Karl Mark, Sigmund Freud and Friedrich Nietzsche.
He produced the First English translation of "Death in Vanice" which appeared in "The Dial" in 1924.
Burk's first essay "Definition of Man" is his first essay of his collection Language as Symbolic Actions.
Harold Bloom singled out Burke's counterstatement and a rhetoric of motives for inclusion in his Western Canon. Major Works of Burke: 1. Counter Statement (1931)

Alexei Maximovich Peshkov who is primarily known as Maxim Gorky was a Russian writer and a founder of Socialist Realism literary method.
Gorky's most famous works are: "The Lower Depths" (1902), "Twenty-Six Men and a Girl", "The Song of the Stormy Petrel", "The Mother" "Summerfolk" and "Children of the Sun".
Gorky wrote memoirs of Leo Tolstoy and Anton Chekhov.
He was an active member of the emerging Marxist Social democratic movement.
He wrote for the newspapers under the pseudonym "Jehudiel Khlamida" and Gorky.
Gorky spent most of his years in exile.
Bertolt Brecht's "The Mother" is based on Gorky's "The Mother".

(1895 - 1975)
Mikhail Mikhailovich Bakhtin was a Russian Philosopher, literary critic and semiotician.
He was from the school of Russian Formalism.
His, "Towards a Philosophy of the Act" first published in 1986 in the USSR is regarded as an unfinished work.
In this book, Bakhtin stated that the essay was to contain 4 parts.
Bakhtin introduced an 'architectonic' or 'schematic modal of the human psyche' which consists of the three components:.
I - for Myself.
I - for - the - other.
Other - for - me.
He explained that 'I - for - the Other' is the one through which human beings develops a sense of Identity.
In Problems of Dostoyevsky's Poetics, Bakhtin introduced three important concepts: 1. The concept of Unfinalizable Self.
According to this concept a person is never fully revealed to the world. 2. The Idea of the relationship between Self and Others:.
According to this concept every person is influenced by other in an intertwined way. 3. Concept of "Polyphony":.
According to this concept, if two people disagree at least one of them must be in error.
When Problems of Dostoyevsky's Art was translated into English, Bakhtin added a chapter on The Concept of Carnival.
According to Bakhtin, Carnival is the context in which distinct individual voices are heard, flourished and interacted together.
The Dialogic Imagination by Bakhtin, is a compilation of four essays concerning language and the novel i) Epic and Novel (1941)

In The Dialogic Imagination, Bakhtin introduces the concept of Heteroglossia, Dialogism, Chronotope and Carnivalesque. Heteroglossia: Heteroglossia describes the co-existence of distinct varieties within a single language. It appeared in Bakhtin's essay Discourse in the Novel (1934 - 35). Dialogism: The dialogic work carries a continual dialogue with other works of literature and other authors. It appeared in Bakhtin's essay The Dialogic Imagination. Chronotope: The chronotope is how configurations of time and space are represented in language and discourse. Carnivalesque: It is a term used by Bakhtin which refers to a literary mode that subverts and liberates the assumptions of the dominant style or atmosphere through humour and chaos. It is related with the "Feast of Fools"
The four categories of Carnivalesque sense of the world are : i) Familiar and free interaction between people ii) Eccentric behaviour iii) Carnivalistic misalliances iv) Sacrilegious.
Its important characteristics are a) A liberation from the prevailing truth and established order b) Emphasis on play, parody, pleasure and the body c) The suspension of all hierarchical rank, principles, norms and prohibitions.
Bakhtin was concerned with language or discourse as a social activity.
The Bakhtin School comprised of Bakhtin, Pavel Medvedev and Valentin Voloshinov.
The Bakhtin School used a Russian word "Slovo" which means "Word" to extend to social flavour that would more readily imply utterance or even discourse.
Julia Kristeva's "Intertextuality" is derived from Bakhtin's 'Dialogism' and Saussure's 'Signs'.
In Rabelais and His World, Bakhtin studies the interaction between the social and literary as well as the meaning of the body and the material bodily lower status.

He is also a major figure in Analytic philosophy and one of the founders of the field of "Cognitive Science".

This sentence was composed by Chomsky in his 1958 book "Syntactic Structure" as an example of sentence that is grammatically correct but syntactically nonsensical.

Chomsky Grammar is a containment hierarchy of classes of formal grammars. This hierarchy was described by Chomsky in 1956. Chomsky Hierarchy consists of following levels: 1. Type-0 grammars (Unrestricted grammar) It includes all formal grammars. 2. Type-1 grammars (Context-sensitive grammars)

Williams was a Welsh academic, novelist and critic. He is considered as a left-wing critic.
His writings on politics, culture, the mass media and literature are significant contributions to the Marxist critique of culture and arts.
Williams get wider fame with the publication of Culture and Society (1958) and The Long Revolution (1961). He reconsidered the classic problem of 'Base and Superstructure' in relation to literature.
Williams' The Country and the City, demolished the notion of country life as simple, natural and unadulterated.
Williams challenged the Marxist modal of an economic 'base' determining a cultural 'superstructure' and replaced it with a more flexible modal in which cultural activities themselves are regarded as material and productive process.
Williams was the founder of New Left Review (1960).
Raymond Williams developed a theory of relation between literary work and social classes in terms of homologies that means a correspondence between two or more structures.

10. Writing in Society Dominant, Residual and Emergent.
The concepts of dominant, residual and emergent are drawn from Raymond Williams.
These concepts can give us a framework for understanding the complex and dynamic ways in which a culture operates as it continuously attempts to maintain stability and balance in the face of ever-changing views.
While one perspective tends to be dominant at a given point, other perspectives are also contending for meaning, some older or more residual, some newer or emergent.
The dominant perspectives are the ones that are embodied in the majority of the society (hence termed dominant) - or by its ruling and most powerful class.
Within the dominant values of any culture, there are many elements of the past are being filtered - "re interpreted", diluted, projected - so that they can be incorporate into dominant culture.
If something residual is truly oppositional to the dominant, the dominant tries to forget it or marginalize it. At times dominants are successful and at times not.

Robert Von Ranke Graves (also known as Robert Ranke Graves ) was an English poet, novelist, critic and classicist. He is a war Poet, and a myth critic.
His memoir of his early life, including his role in the 1st World War, Good Bye to All That, and his speculative study of poetic inspiration The White Goddess (1948) have never been out of print.
He earned his living from writing popular historical novels as - I, Claudius (Autobiography of Roman emperor Claudius (1934), King Jesus (1945), The Golden Fleece, Count Belisarius (1938), In Broken Images etc.
In 1934, He was awarded James Tait Black Memorial Prize for I, Claudius and Claudius the God.
He was also a prominent translator of the classical Latin & Ancient Greek texts; his versions of The Twelve Caesars and The Golden Ass.

His another Historical novel Count Belisarius (1938) recounts the career of Byzantine General "Belisarius".
Graves began a relationship with Beryl Hodge (wife of Alan Hodge).

He turned to Science Fiction with Seven Days in New Crete (1949) and The Nazarene Gospel Restored (1953 along with Joshua Padro).
He also wrote Hercules, My Shipmate in 1945 which was first published as The Golden Fleece (1944).
In 1955, he published The Greek Myths which retells a large body of Greek Myths, each tale followed by extensive commentary drawn from the system of The White Goddess.
He published a volume of short stories like Catacrok: Mostly stories, Mostly Funny (1956)
In 1967, Robert Graves published together with Omar Ali Shah a new translation of Rubaiyat of Omer Khayam.
The Gravestone of Grave is written by his friend and fellow poet Wilfred Owen in Poet's corner at Westminster Abbey.
The Gravestone reads - "My Subject is War, and the pity of War. The poetry is in the pity".

He is famous for his coming-of-age novel "Funny Boy" (1994). It won him Books in Canada first Novel award.

He recounted an account of the discomfort he and his partner experienced during a period spent in Sri Lanka in 1997 in his essay "Coming Out".
In 2004 he edited a collection of short stories "Story Wallah: Short fiction from South Asian Writers" which includes works by Salman Rushdie, Monica Ali, Hanif Kureishi among others.
He published a young adult novel "Swimming in the Monsoon Sea" in 2005. In 2014 he released his fourth novel "The Hungry Ghosts".
In 2013 Shyam's "Funny Boy" was included in the syllabus under marginalized study and gay literature of the under graduation English Department of American College in Madurai.

(1856- 1939)
Sigmund Freud (born as Sigismund Schlomo Freud) was an Austrian neurologist now known as "Father of Psychoanalysis" .
In the words of W. H. Auden " A whole climate of opinion / under whom we conduct our different lives."
Freud read William Shakespeare throughout his life.
In 1895, he published Studies on Hysteria (co-authored with Josef Breuer). Freud described the evolution of his clinical methods and set out his theory of Psychogenetic origins of hysteria, demonstrated in a number of case histories.
In 1899, he published The Interpretation of Dream (1900) in which following a critical review of existing theory, Freud gives detailed interpretations of his own and his patient's dreams in terms of wish fulfilments made subject to the repression and censorship of the "Dream Work".
An abridged version "On Dreams" was published in 1901.
In works which would win him a more general readership, Freud applied his theories outside the clinical setting in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life (1901) and Jokes and their Relation to the Unconscious (1905).
In The Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Freud elaborates his theory of infantile sexuality describing its "Polymorphous Perverse" forms and the junctioning of the "Drives" to which it gives rise in formation of sexual identity.
Freud published a paper entitled "The History of the Psychoanalytic Movement" (1917) the German original being first published in 'Jahrbuch' giving his view on birth and evolution of psychoanalytic movement.
In 1930, Freud was awarded the Goethe Prize in recognition of his contributions to Psychology and to German literary culture.
He worked on his last book Moses and Monotheism published in German in 1938 and in English the following year and the incomplete Outline of Psychoanalysis which was published posthumously.
Freud proposed that the human psyche could be divided into three parts:.
Id.
Ego and.
Superego.
Freud discussed this model in 1920, essay - "Beyond the Pleasure Principle" and fully elaborated upon it in "The Ego and the Id" (1923)
The Id is the completely unconscious, impulsive childlike portion of the psyche that operates on 'Pleasure Principle', in the source of basis impulses and drives.
Freud acknowledged that his use of the term Id, the rational Ego attempts to exact a balance in Id and Superego.
The concept is usually represented by Iceberg model. This model represents the roles of the Id, Ego and Superego, play in relation to conscious and unconscious thought.
Freud's theories also influenced the Frankfurt School and Critical theory as a whole.
Hermeneutics is originally applied to the interpretation of scripture. It is the theory and methodology of text interpretation especially the interpretation of biblical texts, wisdom literature and philosophical texts.

Simone Lucie Ernestine Marie Bertrand de Beauvoir was a French writer and feminist, famous for her notable ideas like.
Ethics of Ambiguity (It is in three parts - Part I: Ambiguity and Freedom. Part II: Personal Freedom and Others. Part III: The Antinomies of Action.)
Feminist Ethics.
Existential Feminism.
She is better known for her 1949 treatise The Second Sex, a detailed analysis of women's oppression and a fundamental tract of contemporary feminism.
She is also known for her open relationship with Jean-Paul Sarte.
She published her first novel She Came to Stay in 1943. It was a fictionalized chronicle of her and Sarte's sexual relationship.
In 1944 de Beauvoir wrote her first existentialist essay "Pyrrhus et Cineas: A Discussion on an Existentialist Ethics". She wrote second existentialist essay "The Ethics of Ambiguity" (1947).
The Second Sex (1949) published in French sets out a feminist existentialism which prescribes a moral revolution.
As an existentialist de Beauvoir believed that existence precedes essence; hence one is not born a woman but becomes a woman.
In the chapter 'Women: Myth and Reality" of The Second Sex, de Beauvoir argued that men had made women the "Other" in the society by application of a false aura of 'mystery' around them.
Her important works are:.
She Came to Stay (1943)
Pyrrhus et Cineas (1944, non-fiction),.
Who Shall Die (1945),.
All Men Are Mortal (1946),.
The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), etc.

(1943-)
Stephan Jay Greenblatt is an American literary critic, theorist, scholar and Pulitzer Prize winning author.
He is the editor of the 'Norton Shakespeare' (2015) and a contributor to the Norton Anthology of English Literature.
He is regarded as the founder of New Historicism in 1980's.
He is the co-founder of the literary cultural journal - 'Representations'.
His most popular work is Will in the World, a biography of Shakespeare.
He won Pulitzer Prize in 2012 for "General Non-Fiction'.
He was born in Boston and was raised in Cambridge.
"Practicing New Historicism" is a combined writing of Greenblatt and Catherine Gallagher in 2010.
Greenblatt first used New Historicism in 1980 in his "Introduction to the Power of Forms in the English Renaissance".
In practising the New Historicism Stephan Greenblatt and Catherine Gallagher focused on five central aspects of new historicism 1. Recurrent use of anecdote 2. Pre-occupation with the nature of representations 3. Fascination with the history of the body 4. Sharp focus on neglected details and 5. Sceptical analysis of ideology.
Greenblatt introduced the terms "Resonance" and "Wonder" in his essay "Romance and Wonder" where he defined "Resonance" as.
The power of the displayed object to reach out beyond its formal boundaries to a larger world, to evoke in the viewer the complex dynamic cultural forces from which it has emerged and for which it may be taken by a viewer to stand.
He defined "Wonder" as.
The power of the displayed object to stop the viewer in his or her tracks, to convey an arresting sense of uniqueness to evoke an exalted attention.
He also introduced "Self Fashioning" in his book Renaissance and Self-Fashioning. This term signifies "A willingness to ... transform oneself into another. Stephan Greenblatt's The Circulation of Social Energy.
In his essay "The Circulation of Social Energy" Stephan Greenblatt shows, how a work written by a dead author of a dead culture can still be relevant today, through what he described as "Social Energy" or the process of cultural action or change.
To interpret a work through New Historicism we need to ask the following questions; (i) Who is the writer of the text? (ii) What provoked him to write? (iii) What are the series of events that are happening during his time? (iv) What was his intention of writing the text? etc..
New Historicism challenged Formalism, structuralism and De-construction theories.

Viktor Shklovsky was a Russian formalist, literary theorist, critic, writer and pamphleteer.
During the first world war he volunteered for the Russian army and eventually become a driving trainer in an armoured car unit in St. Petersburg.
In 1916, he founded OPOYAZ (Society for the Study of Poetic Language). It was a prominent group of linguists and literary critics in St. Petersburg which includes Viktor Shklovsky, Boris Eikhenbaum, Osip Brik, and Yury Tynianov.
He participated in February revolution of 1917. Subsequently the Russian provisional government sent him as an assistant commissioner to southern front where he was wounded and got an award for bravery.
In Berlin 1923, he published his memoirs about the period 1917-1922 under the title Sentimental Noe Puteshutve Vospominanita (A Sentimental Journey), alluding to A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy by Laurence Stern.
In 1923, he wrote his epistolary novel 200 or Letters Not About Love.
Shklovsky was best known for developing the concept of Ostranenie or Defamiliarization.
He explained this concept in the important essay "Art as Technique" (translated as Art as Device) which comprised the first chapter of his seminal Theory of Prose first published in 1925.

The term was coined by Viktor Shklovsky is his essay Art as Technique (Art as Device) in 1917.
He invented the term as a means to distinguish poetic language from practical language on the basis of former's (poetic) perceptibility.
He stated that poetic language is fundamentally different than the language we use every day and thus more difficult to understand.
Poetic speech is framed speech, while prose is ordinary.
He introduced this term in opposition to Russian Symbolist Theories of Art.
According to Shklovsky, 'defamiliarization is, by disrupting the modes of ordinary linguistic discourse, literature makes strange the world of everyday perception and renews the readers lost capacity for fresh sensation'.

Humbert Humbert describes the death of his childhood sweetheart Annabel Leigh.

Humbert marries Charlotte so that he can be near to Lolita all the time. He plans to rape Lolita in a hotel by giving her sleeping pills.

Lolita is found missing, her mother Catherine is dead and Humbert develops a new relationship with a woman named Rita.
He gets a letter from Lolita who is now 17, married and pregnant and desperate in need of money.
Humbert goes to see her, giving her money in exchange for the name of the man who abducted her as Clare Quality.

She married Dick. She refused to go with Humbert.
Humbert meets Quilty and shoots him dead.
He is arrested for driving on the wrong side.
The narrative closes with Humbert's final words to Lolita in which he wishes her will, and reveals the novel in its metafiction to be memoirs of his life, only to be published after his and Lolita's death.

The intentional Fallacy is derived from "confusion between the poem and its origins".
Essentially it occurs, when a critic puts too much emphasis on personal, biographical or external information when analysing a work.
Intentional Fallacy is claimed to be the error of interpreting an evaluating a literary work by reference of evidence, outside the text itself, for the intention - the design and purpose of its author.
It was first published in 'The Sewanee Review' (1946).

They defined Affective Fallacy as "The error of evaluating a poem by its effects - especially its emotional effects - upon the reader. As a result of this fallacy, "the poem itself as an object of specifically critical judgement, tends to disappear, so that criticism ends in impressionism and relativism". Note: Fallacy means mistake in thinking that keeps us away from real understanding.
